readerTitle: Nobody used more paper towels. So why did the factory get swamped?
caseNote: 가상 장면 (키친타월 진열대, 가사 청소 업체, 사내 장비팀) + 실제 연구 (Lee·Padmanabhan·Whang 1997, MIT 맥주 게임) + 실제 기업 관찰 (P&G 기저귀 주문)
insight: 주문은 수요가 아니다. 공급망의 각 단계는 실제 사용량이 아니라 바로 아래 단계의 주문만 보기 때문에, 작은 변화가 위로 갈수록 큰 파동이 된다.
misconception: 주문이 크게 늘었으면 고객 수요도 그만큼 늘어난 것이다. 넉넉히 주문하는 것은 나만 안전해지는 공짜 보험이다.

sources.text: Lee, H. L., Padmanabhan, V., & Whang, S. (1997). The Bullwhip Effect in Supply Chains. Sloan Management Review, 38(3).
Sterman, J. D. (1989). Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision Making Experiment. Management Science, 35(3). (MIT 맥주 게임)
차트와 판단 문제의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: P&G 기저귀(Pampers) 주문 변동 사례는 Lee·Padmanabhan·Whang(1997)에 소개된 내용입니다. 카드에는 '1990년대', '소매 → 유통 → P&G → 공급사로 갈수록 변동이 커졌다'는 일반적인 서술만 썼습니다. 원문 표현을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
맥주 게임: 4단계 공급망(소매·도매·유통·공장), 고객 수요가 한 번만 계단식으로 바뀌는데도 상류 주문이 크게 출렁인다는 결과는 Sterman(1989) 기준입니다. 참가자에 경험 있는 관리자도 포함되었다는 점을 확인하세요.
차트 수치(소비자 +10%, 매장 +25%, 유통 +50%, 제지 공장 +100%)는 증폭 모양을 보여주기 위한 가상 수치입니다.
청소 업체 계산: 평소 월 100병 × 예약 20% 증가 = 120병. 2주 배송 대기분은 '작은 추가분'으로만 표현했습니다.
4가지 원인(수요 신호 처리, 묶음 주문, 가격 변동, 배급 시 과다 주문)은 Lee 외(1997)의 분류를 쉬운 말로 옮긴 것입니다.

cards.title: Nobody used more paper towels.
body: A shopper sees a half-empty shelf and takes two packs instead of one. A few others do the same. The store's sales jump, so it orders extra from its distributor, plus a bit more to be safe.

The distributor sees that spike from many stores and orders even more from the mill. By the time the signal reaches the factory, it looks like a boom. At home, people are using paper towels exactly as before.

image.label: Half-empty paper towel shelf with a shopper holding two packs
image.brief: 마트 키친타월 진열대가 절반쯤 비어 있고, 손님 한 명이 두 팩을 안고 있는 장면. 뒤쪽으로 트럭과 공장이 점점 크게 이어지며 커지는 물결 모양 화살표. 실제 브랜드 로고나 포장 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Spring bookings jumped. How much do you reorder?
body: You run a home-cleaning company with eight crews. Bookings rose 20% this month, the usual spring bump. Your supply room is low, and deliveries take two weeks.
You normally order 100 bottles of cleaner a month. What do you order now?

options.text: 200 bottles. Running out would be worse than overstocking
options.feedback: You won't run out, but you've doubled your order on a 20% rise. Your supplier now sees a doubling, and you sit on cleaner well into summer.

options.text: About 120, plus a small top-up to cover the two-week wait
options.feedback: This tracks what customers actually booked. You stay covered without sending your supplier a signal much bigger than reality.
No overstock, but crews may run short mid-month. Ignoring a real rise is the opposite mistake.

cards.title: A small ripple becomes a big wave.
body: Back to the paper towels. Shoppers bought 10% more for a few weeks. Each link ordered based on what it saw from the link below, plus a cushion of its own.

groups.label: Rise in orders vs a normal month

cards.callout: Then shoppers stop. Everyone holds extra stock, and orders crash below normal all the way up.

cards.title: The bullwhip effect
body: The **bullwhip effect** is when small changes in what end customers buy grow into big swings in orders further up the supply chain.

A small flick of the wrist sends the tip of a whip flying. Each business sees only the orders from the link below it, not real use. So it reacts to a signal that's already exaggerated, and adds its own.

image.label: A whip whose wave grows from shopper to store to distributor to factory
image.brief: 가로로 긴 채찍 일러스트. 손잡이 쪽에 'Shoppers', 이어서 'Store', 'Distributor', 끝부분에 'Factory' 라벨. 손잡이 쪽 물결은 작고 끝으로 갈수록 크게 휘어짐.

cards.softwareNote: Software teams see it in cloud capacity. Each team pads its request, the platform team pads the total, and the company commits to far more servers than anyone uses.

cards.title: Big companies found it in their own data.
body: In the 1990s, Procter & Gamble studied its diaper business. Babies use diapers at a steady rate. Yet store orders swung, distributor orders swung more, and P&G's orders to its own suppliers swung most. Hau Lee, V. Padmanabhan and Seungjin Whang described this in a 1997 paper.
MIT's **beer game** shows it in a classroom. Players run a four-step chain. Customer demand changes just once, yet orders upstream swing wildly, even with experienced managers playing.

cards.title: Four habits that crack the whip.
body: Each one makes sense on its own. Together they amplify.
list: **Reacting to orders, not use:** a jump in orders looks like a trend, so you raise your forecast
**Ordering in batches:** monthly or full-truck orders turn smooth demand into lumps
**Price deals:** a discount makes buyers stock up now and order nothing later
**Fear of shortage:** when supply is rationed, buyers ask for more than they need
cards.callout: The fixes run the other way: share real demand, order smaller and more often, keep prices steady.
cards.softwareNote: In a digital business, watch signups driven by a launch or a discount. A spike in trials is an order, not lasting use. Hiring support staff on the spike can leave you overstaffed a month later.

cards.title: Not every spike is noise.
body: Calming the whip doesn't mean ignoring orders. Sometimes demand really has changed, and the business that waits for proof runs out.

The fixes have costs too. Sharing your sales data takes trust, and a supplier may use it in price talks. Smaller, more frequent orders can cost more to ship. Dampening the swings pays off when the swings cost more than the fixes.

cards.title: Now you run the laptop team.
body: You manage equipment for a 2,000-person company. Last quarter laptops ran short and some new hires waited a week for one.
This quarter, department requests are up 60%. The company's hiring plan is up 10%. What do you do?

image.label: Stack of laptop request forms next to a small hiring chart
image.brief: 사무실 책상 위에 노트북 요청서가 높이 쌓여 있고, 옆 모니터에는 완만하게 오르는 채용 계획 그래프. 요청서 더미와 그래프 높이 차이가 눈에 띄게. 실제 노트북 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Order 60% more laptops so nobody waits again
options.feedback: Nobody waits, but you'll likely hold hundreds of idle laptops. You're reacting to padded requests, not to hiring.

options.text: Plan from the hiring plan, keep a small buffer, and show managers live stock so they stop padding
options.feedback: You order on real use and remove the fear that caused the padding. It takes effort to get hiring data, but the swings shrink.

options.text: Order 15% more and split it in proportion to each request
options.feedback: It caps the cost, but splitting by request size rewards whoever asked for most. Next quarter, requests grow even more.

cards.title: Order on what customers use, not on what others order.
body: Every link that pads its order distorts the view of the next. Look past the order to the real use behind it.
**Try it today:** pick one thing you reorder often. Compare your last three orders with what you actually used in those months.
